<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document" style="font-size:173%;">Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowds
<br class="ltx_break">via Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Deploying mobile robots safely among humans requires the motion planner to account for the uncertainty in the other agents’ predicted trajectories. This remains challenging in traditional approaches, especially with arbitrarily shaped predictions and real-time constraints.
To address these challenges, we propose a Dynamic Risk-Aware Model Predictive Path Integral control (DRA-MPPI), a motion planner that incorporates uncertain future motions modelled with potentially non-Gaussian stochastic predictions. By leveraging MPPI’s gradient-free nature, we propose a method that efficiently approximates the joint Collision Probability (CP) among multiple dynamic obstacles for several hundred sampled trajectories in real-time via a Monte Carlo (MC) approach.
This enables the rejection of samples exceeding a predefined CP threshold or the integration of CP as a weighted objective within the navigation cost function. Consequently, DRA-MPPI mitigates the freezing robot problem while enhancing safety. Real-world and simulated experiments with multiple dynamic obstacles demonstrate DRA-MPPI’s superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, including Scenario-based Model Predictive Control (S-MPC), Frenét planner, and vanilla MPPI.
Videos of the experiments can be found at <a href="https://autonomousrobots.nl/paper_websites/dra-mppi" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://autonomousrobots.nl/paper_websites/dra-mppi</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mobile robots have the potential to enhance various aspects of daily life, from optimizing logistics in warehouses to enabling safer and more efficient transportation through autonomous vehicles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. However, for robots to be successfully integrated into real-world settings like urban areas, they must be capable of safely and efficiently manoeuvring through human-populated spaces. Achieving this requires an ability to interpret and anticipate human movement—a task complicated by the inherent unpredictability of human behaviour. Prediction models, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, provide probabilistic distributions over potential human trajectories. To ensure safe and efficient navigation, these probabilistic predictions must be incorporated into the motion planning process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A key challenge in planning under uncertainty is finding a safe trajectory despite the stochastic nature of surrounding obstacles. One approach to handle uncertainty in dynamic environments is <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">robust optimization</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, which enforces safety guarantees by considering worst-case scenarios within bounded uncertainty sets. This method assumes that the probability density of uncertainty is nonzero within a defined region of the ego agent’s workspace, ensuring strict safety constraints. However, by accounting for all possible uncertainty realizations, robust optimization often leads to overly cautious behaviour, potentially rendering solutions infeasible in densely populated environments—a phenomenon commonly referred to as the “frozen robot” problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. To mitigate excessive conservatism, <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">stochastic optimization</span> offers an alternative by employing chance constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> that probabilistically bound the likelihood of constraint violations within a specified confidence level <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. This relaxation allows for more flexible decision-making while maintaining a controlled level of risk, enabling robots to navigate complex environments more effectively than purely robust approaches.
In this work, we propose a risk-aware Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) that uses Monte-Carlo sampling to approximate the chance constraints for a mobile robot navigating among dynamic agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In stochastic optimization, constraint violations are regulated using chance constraints, which ensure that the probability of satisfying a given nominal constraint remains within a predefined threshold. Evaluating chance constraints exactly is often infeasible in real-world scenarios, necessitating approximations. Many existing methods address this challenge by introducing simplifying assumptions, such as modelling uncertainty with Gaussian distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> or restricting the robot’s dynamics to linear systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. While these approximations facilitate tractability, they also limit the flexibility of the approach. Recent research has made significant progress in overcoming these limitations, enabling stochastic optimization to accommodate nonlinear robot dynamics and more general uncertainty distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> by leveraging scenario optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>. However, the Collision Probability (CP) in these works is computed per obstacle, which degrades performance when
more obstacles influence the plan, i.e., in crowded environments. In addition, empirical evaluations indicate that the <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">actual risk</span> associated with the planned trajectory is significantly lower than the upper bound imposed by the chance constraint formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. To address this issue, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> introduced a method to quantify the risk of planned trajectories by running multiple probabilistic planners in parallel with varying risk thresholds. This approach provides probabilistic safety guarantees by attaining a closer bound to the specified risk. However, the scalability of this approach is constrained by the number of probabilistic planners that can be executed in parallel.
With the advantage of not requiring gradient information, probabilistic safety measures have been successfully employed in sampling-based motion planning frameworks. In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, chance constraints are applied to the Rapidly Random Trees (RRT) algorithm such that each node in the tree is statistically safe. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> integrates risk measures to estimate the risk of violating a predefined safety
specification into a sampling-based trajectory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> to plan minimal risk trajectories.
Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI), a gradient-free local motion planner, has the advantage of massive parallelizability to compute finite horizon plans online via sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> integrates the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) measure into MPPI to generate optimal control actions but only accounts for the uncertainty in the robot’s own dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI (DRA-MPPI), a planner approximating joint CPs among several dynamic obstacles by evaluating the probabilistic distributions of dynamic agents’ predicted trajectories, which can be non-Gaussian. The approximated probability of collision becomes a chance constraint by assigning a high enough cost to samples that violate the maximum threshold, essentially rejecting them from the final plan. Leveraging Monte Carlo (MC) sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> enables greater flexibility and computational efficiency, as it effectively handles arbitrary probability distributions and scales well with an increasing number of dynamic agents.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Contributions</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are twofold:</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DRA-MPPI: An MPPI-based planner that approximates the CPs of trajectories using MC methods. It handles joint CPs over several dynamic obstacles and manages non-Gaussian predictions with minimal approximations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A computationally efficient strategy to find the MC approximation of the joint CP for several hundred samples in parallel, achieving real-time performance.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We design a comprehensive cost function for efficient navigation and validate the approach through simulations and real-world experiments with pedestrians. Our method, tested with Gaussian and non-Gaussian models, is compared to a state-of-the-art Scenario-based Model Predictive Control (S-MPC), a risk-aware Frenét planner, and a vanilla MPPI.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Preliminaries</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a controlled robot moving in a 2D plane, <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, with non-linear discrete-time dynamics given by:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{t}=\left[\bm{q}_{t},\psi_{t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{t}=\left[\bm{q}_{t},\psi_{t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the state and control input of the robot at stage <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. The state of the robot <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> contains its position <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{q}_{t}=[x_{t},y_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{q}_{t}=[x_{t},y_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> and orientation <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The robot navigates in an environment occupied by <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> dynamic obstacles whose future trajectories must be predicted. This necessitates a dynamic model of the obstacles’ motion, enabling the robot to proactively account for the obstacles’ behaviour while generating its own trajectory.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">III-A</span> </span><span id="S3.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dynamic Obstacle Model</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The motion planner uses a model that probabilistically forecasts the behaviour of surrounding agents. In this setting, we model the positions of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> dynamic obstacles as random variables. Specifically, the uncertain position of obstacle <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math> at time step <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\delta}^{o}_{t}=[x_{t}^{o},y_{t}^{o}]\in\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\delta}^{o}_{t}=[x_{t}^{o},y_{t}^{o}]\in\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> is the probability space capturing the uncertainty in the perception of these obstacles. This uncertainty is characterized by a probability measure <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℙ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{P}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To capture the inherent multi-modality in obstacle behaviour, we model the uncertainty in their motion using a Mixture-of-Gaussians (MoG) distribution. This approach provides a flexible and expressive representation of uncertainty by combining multiple continuous probability distributions. Specifically, the probability density function of an obstacle’s position at time step <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is given by:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}^{o}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{m}}\phi_{i}p_{t,i}^{o}(x,y)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}^{o}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{m}}\phi_{i}p_{t,i}^{o}(x,y),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of modes of the MoG, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the weight associated with each mode such that <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{N_{m}}\phi_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msubsup><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{N_{m}}\phi_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the probability density function of the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i^{\text{th}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>i</mi><mtext>th</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i^{\text{th}}</annotation></semantics></math> mode with mean <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and covariance <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{i}(t),\bm{\Sigma}_{i}(t))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)=\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{i}(t),\bm{\Sigma}_{i}(t)).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">As a result, the prediction model outputs a sequence of state distributions over the prediction horizon for each possible mode, enabling the planner to account for the stochastic nature of obstacle motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">III-B</span> </span><span id="S3.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Probabilistic Collision Avoidance</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The problem of planning under uncertainty can be formulated as a chance-constraint collision avoidance problem. Given a cost function <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, the initial state of the robot <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{x}_{\text{{init}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mtext>init</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{x}_{\text{{init}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the predicted future states of all obstacles <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t,i}^{o}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> over a horizon <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, the objective is to compute optimal control inputs that guide the robot from its initial state to progress along a reference path, while the collision probability with any moving obstacle at each stage <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is below an acceptable threshold <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. The resulting optimization problem is given by:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody><tr id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_eqn_row"><td class="ltx_eqn_cell" colspan="5"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4.1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\min_{\bm{u}\in\mathbb{U}}\quad" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>𝒖</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝕌</mi></mrow></munder><mspace style="width:1.167em;" width="1.167em"></mspace></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\min_{\bm{u}\in\mathbb{U}}\quad</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}J_{t}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})+J_{T}(\bm{x}_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}J_{t}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})+J_{T}(\bm{x}_{T})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4a)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4.2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S3.E4.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">s.t.</span></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{x}_{\text{init}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mtext>init</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{x}_{\text{init}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4b)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4.3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t}),\quad\bm{x}\in\mathbb{X},\bm{u}\in\mathbb{U}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝕏</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝒖</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝕌</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t}),\quad\bm{x}\in\mathbb{X},\bm{u}\in\mathbb{U},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4c)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4.4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[||\bm{q}_{t}-\bm{\delta}_{t}^{o}||_{2}&gt;r,\forall o\right]\geq 1-\sigma,\forall t," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ℙ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[||\bm{q}_{t}-\bm{\delta}_{t}^{o}||_{2}&gt;r,\forall o\right]\geq 1-\sigma,\forall t,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4d)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{t}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{t}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> represents the stage cost of the robot, and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J_{T}(\bm{x}_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J_{T}(\bm{x}_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the terminal cost. States <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and inputs <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are bounded by the state and input constraint sets <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝕏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{X}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝕌</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{U}</annotation></semantics></math>, and radius <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is the sum of the robot and obstacle radii.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">III-C</span> </span><span id="S3.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Model Predictive Path Integral Control (MPPI)</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> is a sampling-based optimization method for solving stochastic optimal control problems. We consider a discrete-time dynamical system governed by the state-transition equation:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{v}_{t})\quad\bm{v}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{t},\Sigma)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒗</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi>𝒗</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{v}_{t})\quad\bm{v}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{u}_{t},\Sigma),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math> represents a nonlinear state-transition function that dictates the evolution of the state <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒙</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}</annotation></semantics></math> over discrete time steps <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. The control input <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{v}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒗</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{v}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> follows a Gaussian distribution centered at the commanded input <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> with covariance
<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. To generate potential system trajectories, a set of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> perturbed control sequences sequences <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is sampled and rolled-out through the model <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, producing <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding state trajectories <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{k},k\in[0,K-1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{k},k\in[0,K-1]</annotation></semantics></math>, over a planning horizon of length <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>. Given the state trajectories <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and a predefined cost function <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> to be minimized, the total state-cost <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>
for each sampled sequence <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed by evaluating <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{k}=\mathcal{C}(X_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{k}=\mathcal{C}(X_{k})</annotation></semantics></math>. An importance-sampling weighting scheme is then employed to approximate the optimal control sequence. The weight <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> associated with trajectory <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed using an inverse exponential function of the cost <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, adjusted by a tuning parameter <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> known as the inverse temperature:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{k}=\frac{1}{\eta}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\beta}(S_{k}-\rho)\right),\quad\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}=1." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>η</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.000em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{k}=\frac{1}{\eta}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\beta}(S_{k}-\rho)\right),\quad\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}=1.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Here, the minimum sampled cost <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\min_{k}S_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\min_{k}S_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is introduced to enhance numerical stability, and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> is a normalization factor ensuring weights sum to unity. The final control input sequence <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is then computed as a weighted sum of the sampled control sequences:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}V_{k}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}V_{k}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.4" class="ltx_p">Once the optimal control sequence <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained, only the first control input <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{0}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝒖</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{0}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is applied to the system. The procedure is then repeated at the next time step, where, at the next iteration, a time-shifted <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is used as a warm-start.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">III-D</span> </span><span id="S3.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Risk Assessment</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify risk in the context of pedestrian-robot interactions, we define a risk metric that assesses the likelihood of collision. Let <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the set of random variables capturing the uncertainty in pedestrian motion in the <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> directions. The risk metric is a function <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta:\mathcal{Z}\mapsto\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ζ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta:\mathcal{Z}\mapsto\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> that maps these random variables to a real value corresponding to the collision probability. The probability of collision with an obstacle <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math>, the <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginal</span> probability, is then expressed as:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}_{t}^{o}(\bm{q}_{t})=\iint_{x_{t},y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}}p_{t}^{o}(x_{t},y_{t})dxdy,\forall{t},o," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∬</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}_{t}^{o}(\bm{q}_{t})=\iint_{x_{t},y_{t}\in\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}}p_{t}^{o}(x_{t},y_{t})dxdy,\forall{t},o,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where the integration domain <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∘</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as a circular region, with radius <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, centered at the planned robot pose <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{q}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{q}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> at stage <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> along the planning horizon.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, the probability of colliding with at least one obstacle is given by the <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">joint</span> collision probability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. Since, at each time step <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginal</span> probabilities can be assumed independent, the <span id="S3.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">joint</span> collision probability can be computed using a multiplicative approach:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}_{t}(\bm{q}_{t})=1-\prod_{o}^{N_{o}}(1-\mathcal{P}_{t}^{o}(\bm{q}_{t}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∏</mo><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}_{t}(\bm{q}_{t})=1-\prod_{o}^{N_{o}}(1-\mathcal{P}_{t}^{o}(\bm{q}_{t}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Proposed Approach</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the risk associated with the robot’s optimal trajectory in MPPI, <a href="#S3.E8" title="In III-D Risk Assessment ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#S3.E9" title="Equation 9 ‣ III-D Risk Assessment ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> must be evaluated for each sample and each time step in the horizon. For example, with <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=400</annotation></semantics></math> MPPI samples and a horizon <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=20</annotation></semantics></math>, we must compute the collision probability <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8000</annotation></semantics></math> times at each controller iteration. Computing these analytically is not feasible if the controller is to run in real-time. In <a href="#S4.SS1" title="IV-A Monte Carlo Approximation ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-A</span></a>, we propose a Monte Carlo approximation to estimate the <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">joint</span> collision probability for many trajectories efficiently and in parallel. The cost function used to evaluate MPPI samples is detailed in <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B Cost Formulation ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a>, and an overview of the algorithm is presented in <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Algorithm ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Monte Carlo Approximation</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose an algorithm to compute all <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> integral approximations for all <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> samples efficiently and in parallel, allowing good scalability with the number of dynamic obstacles and samples. The process begins by sampling <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{mc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{mc}</annotation></semantics></math> Monte Carlo coordinates from a rectangular collision region <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\square}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em" mathvariant="normal">□</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\square}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is bounded as follows:</p>
<table id="S4.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\square}}_{t}=\{(x,y)\mid x_{\text{lower}}\leq x\leq x_{\text{upper}},y_{\text{lower}}\leq y\leq y_{\text{upper}}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em" mathvariant="normal">□</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>lower</mtext></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>upper</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>lower</mtext></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>upper</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\square}}_{t}=\{(x,y)\mid x_{\text{lower}}\leq x\leq x_{\text{upper}},y_{\text{lower}}\leq y\leq y_{\text{upper}}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The bounds of this region are determined by the minimum and maximum spatial positions of the robot’s states across all rollouts <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> at time step <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, extended by the radius <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\text{lower}}=\min_{k}(x_{k,t})-r,\quad x_{\text{upper}}=\max_{k}(x_{k,t})+r" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>lower</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>k</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>upper</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>k</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\text{lower}}=\min_{k}(x_{k,t})-r,\quad x_{\text{upper}}=\max_{k}(x_{k,t})+r</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{\text{lower}}=\min_{k}(y_{k,t})-r,\quad y_{\text{upper}}=\max_{k}(y_{k,t})+r." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>lower</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>k</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>upper</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>k</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{\text{lower}}=\min_{k}(y_{k,t})-r,\quad y_{\text{upper}}=\max_{k}(y_{k,t})+r.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> robot’s position for rollout <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> at timestep <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. By taking the
minimum and maximum values as bounds and extending the area with the integral radius <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, we cover
the whole area where we need to approximate the integrals at time step <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break">Depending on the obstacles’ trajectory predictions, we get <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{o}\times N_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{o}\times N_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> total number of modes for all obstacles. To approximate the integral for all rollouts <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> we first evaluate the <span id="S4.SS1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">joint</span> collision probability for all MC sample <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}_{j}(x_{j},y_{j})=1-\prod_{o=1}^{N_{o}}(1-p_{t}^{o}(x_{j},y_{j})),\quad\forall j" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>j</mi><mtext>joint</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∏</mo><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>o</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}_{j}(x_{j},y_{j})=1-\prod_{o=1}^{N_{o}}(1-p_{t}^{o}(x_{j},y_{j})),\quad\forall j</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j},y_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j},y_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> represents a single MC sample. We then identify which of these sampled coordinates fall within the region <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> of each <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and compute the CP over the relevant domain:</p>
<table id="S4.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(x_{k,t},y_{k,t})=\frac{\pi r^{2}}{N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{mc}}\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}(x_{j},y_{j})\cdot\mathds{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}(x_{j},y_{j})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></munderover><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>joint</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(x_{k,t},y_{k,t})=\frac{\pi r^{2}}{N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{mc}}\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}(x_{j},y_{j})\cdot\mathds{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}(x_{j},y_{j}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi r^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi r^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the area of the collision region and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of Monte Carlo samples in the circular region <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> acting as a normalization factor. <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathds{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathds{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}</annotation></semantics></math> is an indicator function to consider only MC samples in the circular collision region <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given that all the coordinates <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math> will be fairly close <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall k</annotation></semantics></math>, there will also be significant overlap in the integration regions <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, the computation effort is massively reduced by using our approach of drawing and evaluating the MC samples only once <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall k</annotation></semantics></math>.
The Standard Error (SE) of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}</annotation></semantics></math>, if <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>joint</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}</annotation></semantics></math> were Gaussian distributed, would scale with <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}}}/N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>joint</mtext></msup></msub></msqrt><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msubsup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}}}/N_{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{k,t}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
