In practice, we do not know a priori the number of samples in the collision region, and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>joint</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{\text{joint}}</annotation></semantics></math> is non-gaussian but, compared to an analytical solution, we have empirically observed that we misclassify the CP to be below the threshold less than 2% of the times.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cost Formulation</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key component of MPPI is the design of the cost function <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>. We design our cost function as:</p>
<table id="S4.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{k}=\mathcal{C}_{\text{tracking}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{speed}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{rotation}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>tracking</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>speed</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>rotation</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>risk</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{k}=\mathcal{C}_{\text{tracking}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{speed}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{rotation}}+\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{\text{tracking}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>tracking</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{\text{tracking}}</annotation></semantics></math> drives the robot towards its goal and penalizes the lateral deviation from the reference path, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{\text{speed}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>speed</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{\text{speed}}</annotation></semantics></math> penalizes differences with reference speed, and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{\text{rotation}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>rotation</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{\text{rotation}}</annotation></semantics></math> penalizes angular velocity. <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>risk</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as:</p>
<table id="S4.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}}=\omega_{\text{soft}}\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t})+\omega_{\text{hard}}\mathds{1}_{\sigma}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t}))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mtext>risk</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>soft</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>hard</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{\text{risk}}=\omega_{\text{soft}}\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t})+\omega_{\text{hard}}\mathds{1}_{\sigma}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t})),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\text{soft}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>soft</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\text{soft}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\text{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>hard</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\text{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> being tunable weights.
The first part, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\text{soft}}\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>soft</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\text{soft}}\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t})</annotation></semantics></math>, is a linear penalty on any collision probabilities, incentivising the planner to always choose lower risk.
The second part, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\text{hard}}\mathds{1}_{\sigma}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>hard</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒒</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\text{hard}}\mathds{1}_{\sigma}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\bm{q}_{k,t}))</annotation></semantics></math> is an indicator function returning <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> when the CP is above a chosen risk threshold <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.
Every sampled trajectory with a CP above the threshold, assuming that <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{\text{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ω</mi><mtext>hard</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{\text{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> is high enough and that at least a few low-risk trajectories are sampled, will receive close to zero weight in the average in <a href="#S3.E7" title="In III-C Model Predictive Path Integral Control (MPPI) ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, essentially being rejected.
One advantage is that if, for example, the robot starts planning from a state with CP above the threshold, MPPI still returns a solution in which the CP and the number of time steps with CP above the threshold will be minimised.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Algorithm</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#alg1" title="In IV-C Algorithm ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the proposed approach. Note that operations over <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> are parallelized, while the ones over <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">rolling out</span> the trajectories, are performed sequentially.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> are splines fitted to a Halton sequence for improved smoothness, the inverse temperature <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is updated online, and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is time-shifted to be reused in the next iteration. We also always take one sample to be zero velocity throughout the horizon. This helps MPPI to converge to a braking manoeuvre when all other samples fail <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmrmk1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_rmk">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmrmk1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Remark</span><span id="Thmrmk1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> 1</span></span></h6>
<div id="Thmrmk1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmrmk1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmrmk1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A key difference between MPPI and MPC is that MPPI’s planned trajectory is not meant to be applied in open loop.
When symmetries are present, e.g. when a robot faces an obstacle ahead, MPPI’s plan might go straight through the obstacle. This is intuitively clear given the weighted average in <a href="#S3.E7" title="In III-C Model Predictive Path Integral Control (MPPI) ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
For certain types of systems and cost functions, MPPI can be related to Path Integral Control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
Within the Path Integral control framework, because there is an assumption that the actions of the ego-agent are noisy, attempting to drive straight to the obstacle for a while is the optimal action. The symmetry is proven to break at some point <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.
For our planner, this means that while we can reject the samples <math id="Thmrmk1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> with collision probability higher than the threshold <math id="Thmrmk1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, we cannot guarantee that the resulting plan doesn’t violate the threshold.
Again, this is expected as, in MPPI, only the first input of <math id="Thmrmk1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>U</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is applied, and the rest is only used for warm-starting the next iteration.</span></p>
</div>
</div>

                 <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{k,t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{k,t},\bm{v}_{k,t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒗</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{k,t+1}=\mathcal{F}(\bm{x}_{k,t},\bm{v}_{k,t})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">

</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Simulation Experiments</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section evaluates the proposed approach in the context of mobile robot navigation in a crowded environment shared with humans. Our algorithm’s implementation is built upon previous open-source MPPI solvers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. The proposed approach is developed in Python using PyTorch and integrated with the Robot Operating System (ROS). The laptop running the simulations has an Intel<sup id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">®</sup> Core<sup id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sup">TM</sup> i7 CPU@2.6GHz and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span> </span><span id="S5.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Simulation Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experimental evaluation is conducted in a simulated environment featuring a Clearpath Jackal robot navigating a 6-meter-wide corridor alongside multiple pedestrians. The robot has to follow the corridor’s centerline while maintaining a reference velocity of <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>m/s. A visualization with Gaussian predictions is given in <a href="#S4.F1" title="In IV-C Algorithm ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The simulator runs at <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math>Hz, while the controllers run at <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>Hz.
Pedestrian dynamics are modelled using the Social Forces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, implemented via open-source software <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. In this model, pedestrians avoid one another and the robot. Future pedestrian positions are predicted by the robot’s motion planner using a constant velocity assumption.
The mismatch between the model used for simulation and prediction is to emulate a real-world scenario where the predictions do not always match the ground-truth trajectory.
Pedestrians are modelled with a radius of <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3</annotation></semantics></math>m and spawn on both sides of the corridor, and their goal is to reach the opposing side. The robot dynamics are described by a second-order unicycle model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. Simulations are conducted for three scenarios featuring <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math> pedestrians to evaluate the planner’s performance under varying crowd density levels.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS1.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span>1 </span>Pedestrians with Gaussian noise</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this setup, we model the uncertainty in pedestrian motion using a unimodal Gaussian distribution with covariance matrix <math id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{w}=0.3^{2}\bm{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mn>0.3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝑰</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{w}=0.3^{2}\bm{I}</annotation></semantics></math>. By ‘unimodal’, it is meant that we predict a single trajectory for each pedestrian. We define the pedestrians’ dynamics as:</p>
<table id="S5.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\delta}_{t+1}=\bm{\delta}t+(\bm{v}+\bm{\delta}_{w,t})dt,\quad\bm{\delta}_{w,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{\Sigma}_{w})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝜹</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝒗</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\delta}_{t+1}=\bm{\delta}t+(\bm{v}+\bm{\delta}_{w,t})dt,\quad\bm{\delta}_{w,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{\Sigma}_{w}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒗</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the velocity that follows the social forces model. The additive noise <math id="S5.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\delta}_{w,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\delta}_{w,t}</annotation></semantics></math> introduces stochastic perturbations, capturing the variability in pedestrian motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS1.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span>2 </span>Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this setup, pedestrian motion is modelled as a Markov Chain, where transitions govern changes in the movement direction. Specifically, a pedestrian follows a horizontal trajectory with probability <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.975" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.975</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.975</annotation></semantics></math> at each time step while transitioning to a diagonal trajectory with probability <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.025" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.025</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.025</annotation></semantics></math>. This behaviour is further perturbed by Gaussian noise as before. The pedestrians’ dynamics are described by:</p>
<table id="S5.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\delta}_{t+1}=\bm{\delta}_{t}+(B\bm{v}+\bm{\delta}_{w,t})dt,\quad\bm{\delta}_{w,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{\Sigma}_{w})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒗</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝜹</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\delta}_{t+1}=\bm{\delta}_{t}+(B\bm{v}+\bm{\delta}_{w,t})dt,\quad\bm{\delta}_{w,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{\Sigma}_{w}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> is a transformation vector that depends on the current state of the Markov Chain and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒗</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{v}</annotation></semantics></math> is a constant preferred velocity. If the pedestrian is in the horizontal state, <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=\begin{bmatrix}1&amp;0\end{bmatrix}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt"><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=\begin{bmatrix}1&amp;0\end{bmatrix}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. Conversely, if the pedestrian switches to the diagonal state, <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=\begin{bmatrix}\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}&amp;\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}\end{bmatrix}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">1</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><msqrt><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></msqrt></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">1</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><msqrt><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></msqrt></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=\begin{bmatrix}\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}&amp;\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{2}}}\end{bmatrix}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. The uncertainties associated with this motion can be modelled as a Mixture of Gaussians where each state transition in the Markov Chain leads to a separate mode with an associated probability. For a planning horizon of <math id="S5.SS1.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=20</annotation></semantics></math>, the pedestrian may switch from horizontal to diagonal movement every 5-time steps, resulting in 4 distinct modes per pedestrian.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">V-B</span> </span><span id="S5.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Comparison to Baselines</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare DRA-MPPI against three baselines. Baselines are selected on the availability of an open-source implementation and their application to navigation in 2-D dynamic
environments. We consider the following baselines:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Stochastic Model Predictive Control (SH-MPC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>: This baseline uses a scenario-based MPC and formulates the collision avoidance chance constraints over the entire trajectory as a scenario program.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vanilla MPPI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>: This baseline assumes deterministic pedestrians’ behaviour by considering only the mean predicted trajectories and plans around them.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iii)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Frenét Planner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>: This sampling-based planner generates trajectories in the Frenét coordinate system. The risk metric used is similar to previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All planners have a horizon of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=20</annotation></semantics></math> steps, with a discretization step of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2</annotation></semantics></math>s, resulting in a time horizon of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.0</annotation></semantics></math>s. We set the maximum allowable risk level to <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>. DRA-MPPI uses <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=400</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{mc}=20000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>20000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{mc}=20000</annotation></semantics></math> samples. The following metrics are considered for evaluation:</p>
<ol id="S5.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Task Duration</span>: Measures the time required for the robot to reach the end of the corridor.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Velocity</span>: Determines the average velocity maintained throughout the experiment.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Collision Probability</span>: Quantifies each experiment’s maximum joint collision probability (CP). The CP we report is computed a posteriori. Given the remark in <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Algorithm ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>, the CP is only reported for the current time step instead of over the planned trajectory.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Success Rate (SR)</span>: Evaluates the proportion of experiments in which the robot successfully avoids collisions with pedestrians and reaches its goal.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.21205v2/images/boxplot_timeduration_new.png" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/282;" width="429" height="282" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The visualization illustrates the task duration, defined as the time required to reach the goal, under a uni-modal pedestrian prediction setting. Our method demonstrates a lower variance in task duration and a shorter completion time compared to SH-MPC and the Frenét Planner. While Vanilla MPPI achieves the shortest task duration, this comes at the cost of a higher collision rate, as reported in Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table I ‣ V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.21205v2/images/boxplot_cp_joint_new.png" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/173;" width="429" height="173" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of maximum collision probability across 100 experiments under uni-modal pedestrian prediction setup. Frenét Planner is discarded from this Fig. for better readability as its CP is much higher than SH-MPC and DRA-MPPI as seen in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.21205v2/images/boxplot_mm_td_new.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/170;" width="429" height="170" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of the task duration under multi-modal pedestrian prediction setting. Same conclusions as the uni-modal case.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.21205v2/images/boxplot_cp_mm_new.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/133;" width="429" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Visualization of maximum collision probability across 100 experiments under multi-modal pedestrian prediction setup.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.21205v2/images/rw_interesting.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/117;" width="476" height="117" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Four snapshots of a Jackal robot running DRA-MPPI among five pedestrians. In orange is the trajectory planned by our proposed approach, with the top 30 samples colour-graded by their relative cost. In blue are the predicted trajectories of the pedestrians, and the circle size represents three standard deviations from the mean predicted centre of the obstacle. In green is the reference path. The behaviour is best appreciated in the accompanying video.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T1" title="In V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> and <a href="#S5.F2" title="In V-B Comparison to Baselines ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ V-B Comparison to Baselines ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> present a quantitative comparison of different planning methods across varying pedestrian densities under uni-modal pedestrian predictions. The results, averaged over <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> experiments, highlight the trade-offs between task efficiency and safety among the evaluated approaches.
Our proposed approach (DRA-MPPI) consistently demonstrates a favourable balance between task duration and safety.
While Vanilla MPPI achieves the shortest task duration across all scenarios, it does so at the expense of significantly lower safety due to its lack of risk awareness, particularly as pedestrian density increases.
For instance, in the presence of <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math> pedestrians, Vanilla MPPI completes the task in <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.98" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.98</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.98</annotation></semantics></math>s but exhibits the lowest safety rate (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>43</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43</annotation></semantics></math>%), indicating a high collision frequency.
In contrast, DRA-MPPI maintains a competitive task duration (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19.86</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19.86</annotation></semantics></math>s) while achieving a significantly higher safety rate of <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>98</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98</annotation></semantics></math>%, demonstrating its robustness in crowded environments.
The Frenét Planner exhibits longer task duration and suffers a notable drop in safety, particularly at higher pedestrian densities (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="74\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>74</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74\%</annotation></semantics></math> safety at 12 pedestrians). This deterioration arises from the planner’s design, which does not explicitly optimize for risk minimization. Instead, it evaluates a set of sampled trajectories based on assigned costs and selects the one with the lowest one. However, in dense environments, the trajectory with the minimum cost may still entail substantial risk, as observed in the experimental results.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmrmk2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_rmk">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmrmk2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Remark</span><span id="Thmrmk2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> 2</span></span></h6>
<div id="Thmrmk2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmrmk2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmrmk2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">It is important to stress that, in our simulator, the pedestrians move with Social Forces but are predicted by a constant velocity model, i.e. the predictions are not the ground truth behaviour.
This may result in the planner thinking its plan is below the risk threshold while, at the next iteration, it may find itself at a starting pose with a higher-than-allowed collision probability.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">SH-MPC strives to track the reference path very closely, often finding itself in riskier positions.
SH-MPC relaxes the constraints with slack variables when no feasible solution is found in these riskier situations. When infeasible, SH-MPC switches to a fallback policy (braking). This leads to SH-MPC taking longer to complete the task and often exhibiting collision probabilities higher than the threshold at least a few times per experiment, severely impacting the metrics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Thanks to its cost <a href="#S4.E13" title="In IV-B Cost Formulation ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, DRA-MPPI always minimizes the CP, even when below the threshold. This makes it strive to avoid riskier situations altogether. Moreover, when DRA-MPPI finds itself in a riskier situation, it will try to return to a state with CP below the threshold in the least amount of steps possible.
For these reasons, DRA-MPPI demonstrates good task completion times while providing the highest safety. Moreover, DRA-MPPI and Vanilla MPPI exhibit a lower variance in task duration across experiments, indicating better consistency than SH-MPC and Frenét Planner.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T2" title="In V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a> and <a href="#S5.F4" title="In V-B Comparison to Baselines ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S5.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ V-B Comparison to Baselines ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> show that the key observations from the uni-modal case also hold in the multi-modal setting. DRA-MPPI outperforms other methods in balancing task efficiency and safety. It achieves the shortest task duration (<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19.67" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19.67</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19.67</annotation></semantics></math>s) while maintaining the highest safety rate (<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math>), demonstrating its ability to navigate complex, uncertain environments effectively. In contrast, Vanilla MPPI completes the task in a comparable time (<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19.71</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19.71</annotation></semantics></math>s) but at the cost of reduced safety (<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="78\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>78</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">78\%</annotation></semantics></math>), reflecting its lack of risk-awareness. DRA-MPPI also remains close to the maximum allowable risk while ensuring safety, demonstrating its consistency and robustness in complex pedestrian environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">V-C</span> </span><span id="S5.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Computation Time</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S5.T1" title="In V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table II ‣ V-A2 Pedestrians with Mixture of Gaussians ‣ V-A Simulation Setup ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>, we also report the computation time (runtime) for SH-MPC and our approach. DRA-MPPI takes just below <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math>ms to compute the control action in the uni-modal four-agents experiment, while SH-MPC is almost twice as fast.
Both methods scale quite gracefully over the number of agents with multi-modal predictions.
However, it is important to note that SH-MPC is written in C++, while DRA-MPPI is implemented in PyTorch. Recent work shows a reduction of compute time of up to two orders of magnitude when running MPPI in CUDA vs Pytorch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, highlighting the potential for these massively parallelizable approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Real Robot Experiments</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section demonstrates the DRA-MPPI for a mobile robot driving among pedestrians in an arena, highlighting the real-time capability of the proposed approach.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">VI-A</span> </span><span id="S6.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Experimental Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiment occurs in a large arena where pedestrians walk alongside the robot. The robot and pedestrians’ positions are tracked by a motion capture system operating at 20 Hz. Pedestrian positions are filtered through a Kalman filter that also estimates velocities, which the planner uses to produce constant velocity predictions. The pedestrians are assumed to follow an uni-modal Gaussian distribution with a covariance matrix of <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\Sigma}_{w}=0.1^{2}\bm{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mn>0.1</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝑰</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\Sigma}_{w}=0.1^{2}\bm{I}</annotation></semantics></math>. The robot follows a reference path between two opposite sides of the environment and performs a turn upon reaching each side. The cost function is the same as in <a href="#S4.E13" title="In IV-B Cost Formulation ‣ IV Proposed Approach ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span> </span><span id="S6.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Results</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this set of experiments, the pedestrians were instructed to walk naturally from one side to the other while interacting with the robot. The experiment was conducted over a duration of <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>65</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65</annotation></semantics></math> seconds, with snapshots captured at various time instances, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S5.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ V-B Comparison to Baselines ‣ V Simulation Experiments ‣ Dynamic Risk-Aware MPPI for Mobile Robots in Crowdsvia Efficient Monte Carlo Approximations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Throughout the trials, the maximum collision probability observed for the robot was <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.054" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.054</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.054</annotation></semantics></math>, with an average of <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.023" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.023</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.023</annotation></semantics></math> and a standard deviation of <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.011" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.011</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.011</annotation></semantics></math>. Notably, no collisions were recorded.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusions</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented DRA-MPPI, an MPPI-based planner capable of computing, in parallel, at each time step, the joint collision probability among many dynamic obstacles using potentially non-Gaussian predictions.
Thanks to its gradient-free nature, we have shown that DRA-MPPI can reject samples with a collision probability above a desired threshold and directly minimise the collision probability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In simulated experiments, while the pedestrians were predicted with constant velocity, they moved with Social Forces. DRA-MPPI demonstrated the highest robustness to this mismatch by being the safest method among a Scenario-Based MPC approach, a risk-aware Frenét Planner, and a Vanilla MPPI while maintaining high speed and good task completion times.
Similar conclusions were drawn in experiments where the pedestrians could randomly switch directions, predicted by a Gaussian Mixture Model, demonstrating efficient planning with non-Gaussian distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Real-robot experiments showcased DRA-MPPI’s ease of transfer to the real world and real-time performance. Although we relied on a motion capture system, the pedestrian’s state and the map can be retrieved from onboard sensors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While already real-time, in future work our PyTorch implementation could be rewritten in CUDA, dramatically improving computation times <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>. This could also allow for real-time computations of the Monte Carlo approximation of the joint collision probability over the planning horizon, allowing for accurate constraining of the joint collision probability over the entire trajectory.</p>
</div>
</section>

M. Werling, S. Kammel, J. Ziegler, and L. Groll, “Optimal trajectories for time-critical street scenarios using discretized terminal manifolds,” <em id="bib.bib20.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">The International Journal of Robotics Research</em>, 2012.

</span></li>
      
<li id="bib.bib21" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[21]</span>

</span></li>
      
<li id="bib.bib22" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[22]</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">

<li id="bib.bib23" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[23]</span>

<li id="bib.bib24" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[24]</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">

<li id="bib.bib25" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[25]</span>

<li id="bib.bib26" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[26]</span>

<li id="bib.bib27" class="ltx_bibitem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_bibitem">[27]</span>
